processing: Pu-erh pressed into a heart or mushroom shape with a stem-like knob. Early versions used coarse mature leaf, stems and broken leaf with better leaf on the surface. Raw and ripe versions both exist.
harvest_season: Not tied to a prized picking. Traditionally it used coarser, mature leaf, not early buds, though some recent versions use more bud.
appearance_dry: A compact dark heart-shaped or mushroom-shaped piece, wrapped in paper and usually carrying a Baoyan brand slip.
appearance_liquor: Amber to orange-brown for raw pieces, deepening with age and much darker for ripe ones.
appearance_wet: Coarse mixed leaf and stems in the traditional style, with a higher share of bud in some recent lots.
taste_profile: With coarse leaf you would typically expect a strong, plain cup with wood and some bitterness, which suits boiling. Little dependable tasting detail is recorded, and the taste differs greatly between raw and ripe.

brewing.notes: These pieces are dense, so steam or carefully pry them apart before brewing. They can also be simmered with milk or butter, closer to how they were used in Tibetan areas.

vintage_note: Sold by year and factory, with the Xiaguan Baoyan brand as the reference point. Raw pieces can be drunk young or stored, and ripe ones are ready sooner. Fakes of the heart-shaped Baoyan tuo are common, so buy from a reliable dealer.
description:
Jincha, whose name means roughly tight tea, is Yunnan's heart-shaped compressed tea. Drinkers also call it mushroom tuo, for the knob that sticks out of its underside. It was made for Tibetan areas, where it was boiled for butter tea, and it was never designed as a collector's piece.

That purpose explains the leaf. Early pieces used coarse mature leaf, stems and broken leaf, with nicer leaf on the outside, because it had to stand up to boiling. Some recent Xiaguan pieces use more bud and fewer old stems.

The shape ages more slowly than a flat cake because little surface is exposed. It is also awkward to break, so steam it or work it apart patiently, then brew hot. Check whether you hold raw or ripe, because they are very different teas.

Baoyan is the name to look for, and it is also the one most often copied. It remains the classic, and it costs far less than the old mark cakes.
history:
Jincha is said to have appeared after the tuo, and was aimed at the Tibetan market. One collector's account says the Yunnan tea company gave it the unified Baoyan brand in 1949, and that Menghai, Xiaguan, Jinggu and Yanjin factories all made it at some point.

The same account says all production was assigned to Xiaguan in 1986, after which the Xiaguan Baoyan jincha became a signature product of the factory. These details come from enthusiast writing and have not been confirmed in official histories.
